required_outcomes: Classifies the report from its facts as a routine appliance issue (a single soap-drawer overflow, already mopped up, machine drained, no ongoing leak), not an emergency or an escape of water, and sets the category and priority accordingly.

Replies to the tenant acknowledging the report, giving practical self-checks (clean the soap drawer and its housing, check the detergent type and dose, look for a blockage in the drawer) and asking them to report back if it happens again.
Asks the tenant to confirm there is no water damage or water near sockets or under the units, and no complaint from the flat below.
Takes a routine next step rather than an urgent one: either monitors via the tenant's report back with a dated follow-up, or asks the landlord to approve a routine appliance engineer visit.
acceptable_alternatives: Requesting landlord approval for a routine appliance engineer straight away, at routine priority, while still giving the tenant the self-checks.
Asking the tenant for a photo or short video of the drawer during a wash before deciding on an engineer.
positive_behaviours: Explains to the tenant briefly why this does not need an emergency call-out, and what would make it urgent (water still escaping, water near electrics, a leak through to the flat below).
Records in the case notes that 'flooded' referred to a one-off drawer overflow that has been cleaned up.
red_flags: Escalating to a human as an emergency or P1, or treating the case as an escape of water.
Stalling on the word 'flooded' with no tenant reply and no routine next step.
prohibited_actions: Dispatching an emergency plumber or contractor, or approving spend under an emergency justification.
Telling the tenant to shut off the water main or isolate the electrics as if water were still escaping.
critical_failures: Treating the report as an active flood and sending an emergency contractor without landlord approval.
